content: 1. HCV RNA detection assays have a sensitivity threshold of approximately 1000–3000 IU/mL. 2. Nucleic acid testing (NAT) on plasma and serum samples demonstrates greater sensitivity compared to core antigen (cAg) assays. 3. Published data suggest that qualitative NAT assays are generally more sensitive than quantitative assays, though this may not hold true for newer assay technologies. 4. HCV core antigen testing using immunoassay formats has the potential to be more cost-effective due to lower material costs. 5. HCV core antigen assays are more stable and do not require cold chain storage, making them logistically advantageous. 6. Decentralized testing for active HCV infection can facilitate faster diagnosis and treatment initiation, particularly in resource-limited settings. 7. Both HCV cAg and NAT tests are being developed for use with capillary blood at the point of care, though current cAg immunoassays still require sophisticated laboratory equipment, electricity, and skilled personnel. 8. Some NAT assays are already available for near-patient testing but still require plasma samples. 9. In high-prevalence settings, direct testing strategies without prior antibody testing can identify patients earlier in their infection, reduce loss to follow-up, and enable faster treatment initiation. 10. Patients with low-level viremia (<3000 IU/mL) may be missed by HCV cAg assays or less sensitive NAT methods, though the clinical implications of this are not fully understood. 11. The benefits of HCV cAg testing, such as cost-effectiveness and accessibility, may outweigh the risks in certain settings, particularly where decentralized testing is prioritized. 12. While data exist on the utility of HCV cAg in seronegative individuals, no studies have evaluated its use alongside NAT in one-step diagnostic strategies for key affected populations. 13. Qualitative NAT assays are generally as sensitive or more sensitive than quantitative assays, and their cost may be lower. 14. Recent evidence suggests that monitoring HCV viral load during treatment with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) may not be necessary, as early viral response is not predictive of cure. 15. Baseline viral load quantification may also not be required, though this is not yet widely reflected in clinical guidelines. 16. A survey of implementers and users of hepatitis B and C testing services found that diagnostic sensitivity of >95% was acceptable if the test cost was low, with most respondents favoring a cost below $10 USD. 17. Respondents in lowand middle-income countries preferred decentralized testing and capillary blood-based assays, even at the expense of sensitivity. 18. Half of the surveyed patients preferred test results within two hours, while 27% found same-day results acceptable. 19. Patients at risk of progressive liver disease benefit from reduced morbidity and mortality when treatment is initiated as a result of expanded access to testing programs. 20. Testing and treatment programs can reduce the burden of advanced liver disease, hepatocellular carcinoma, and premature mortality within affected communities. 21. Health-care workers will require training in the use of testing equipment, particularly for near-point-of-care settings, and must ensure proper reporting and recording of results. 22. Laboratories will need training for HCV cAg testing, including careful sample processing to optimize antigen detection. 23. Equity in testing access will improve with reduced costs and increased decentralization, though further efforts are needed to enhance access to testing facilities. 24. Ethical considerations include ensuring equitable access to testing and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings. 25. Resource requirements for implementation include the cost of testing platforms, reagents, transportation of specimens, and training of laboratory staff. 26. New point-of-care or near-point-of-care platforms for HCV RNA testing are under development, which may further improve accessibility. 27. Current HCV cAg testing is most relevant for populations relying on centralized laboratory testing for HCV RNA confirmation. 28. One-step testing strategies using HCV cAg or NAT may only be cost-effective in high-prevalence settings. 29. Recommendations are less applicable in high-income settings with established hepatitis C testing and treatment programs. 30. Research gaps include evaluating one-step diagnostic strategies, understanding outcomes for patients with low viral loads, and optimizing antigen detection in patients with high viral loads but negative cAg results. 31. Further studies are needed to assess the kinetics of HCV cAg during treatment, particularly with new DAA regimens. 32. More rigorous accuracy studies are required, especially in populations with HIV or HBV coinfection or specific HCV genotypes. 33. Development of multiplex instruments for simultaneous diagnosis of HCV, HIV, HBV, and TB in health centers is recommended. 34. Variability in study methodologies, such as unclear participant selection and limited data on certain genotypes, has led to downgrading of evidence quality in some cases. 35. Imprecision in pooled confidence intervals and small sample sizes have also contributed to downgrading of evidence for certain assays. 36. Testing platforms vary in cost, throughput, and time to results, with some capable of processing up to 96 samples in three hours.
